#2594. Six lessons learned from NFL Week 9: Arvell Reese a superstar in the making, C.J. Stroud having career year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the trade deadline today, I am reminded that self-awareness is of one of the best attributes an organization can have, from top to bottom.

The team that comes to mind immediately is one we've heard a lot from -- not in a good way -- this year: the Colts. Around this time last year, Indianapolis sent away two first-round picks for Sauce Gardner in a trade-deadline blockbuster. Indianapolis was 7-2 at the time, but was it really a team that needed to go all-in? No. Daniel Jones was playing so over-his-head well, and a smart front office would have recognized the great record was a product of a very soft schedule, a little bit of luck and an unprecedented hot streak. There was no rush here. The 2025 season was supposed to be a transition one, and a medium-sized cornerback addition would have been fine. Again, just a few months earlier, Indianapolis was basically taking a flyer on Jones.

You know how the rest of the story goes. Jones and the offense start to fall off, then Jones ruptures his Achilles. Now, the Colts are 2-7 and in the midst of a franchise-altering sale while not even owning their first-round pick. If the draft started today, Indianapolis would send the No. 4 pick to the Jets. Yikes!

The Jets, meanwhile, continue to profit in a big way off of that trade and the Quinnen Williams trade. They currently own the No. 4 (Colts'), No. 6 (their own) and No. 13 (Cowboys') picks. They knew this would be a long process. They knew it could be ugly for a while, and this year's 2-7 mark confirms that. But New York could have a terrific kickstart to their rebuild in a few months' time.

One team fell for fool's gold. The other knew exactly where it was and embraced its unenviable role.

The Jets are still waiting to fully invest in their rebuild. The other New York team? Well, it has already started -- and is way ahead of schedule -- thanks to a different type of self-awareness.

Please just watch these highlights first, then pick your jaw up from off the floor and continue reading below.

ARVELL REESE COMPLETELY TOOK OVER AGAINST THE EAGLES.12 TKL, 10 SOLO, 3 SACK, 1 FF vs Eagles.Reese is the DROY favorite and making a case for DPOY consideration. https://t.co/zAwPLEFwnv pic.twitter.com/xJGzta0fCF

The biggest question surrounding Reese during the build-up to the NFL Draft was "Where do you play him?"

The answer should have been another question: "Why does it matter?"

And the Giants were exactly right to take that approach. Reese was an EDGE at Ohio State who moonlighted at off-ball linebacker. When the Giants initially drafted him, John Harbaugh basically said he'd play linebacker but also move around. Through eight games, Reese has now played at least 30 snaps at seven different spots: right inside linebacker, left inside linebacker, right linebacker, right EDGE, left linebacker, middle linebacker and left EDGE.

This is the way the NFL is trending. Think about guys such as Seattle's Nick Emmanwori, technically a safety who really plays everywhere, and someone we've talked about in this column before. Reese is of that ilk: a truly, laughably absurd athlete. A weapon who transcends positional labels. His strip sack of Joe Milton happened in 2.29 seconds, the fastest sack of the year per Next Gen Stats.

Arvell Reese Ladies and Gentlemen #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/BeoQwGZG3A

Here's where the self-awareness portion comes in. The Giants knew neither they nor Reese had to have it figured out on Day 1. The Giants are in Year 1 under John Harbaugh and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson. Reese is 21 years old. The world was (and still is!) their oyster to experiment. Reese looks phenomenal. The Giants are 5-2-1 despite having started three different quarterbacks, and players such as Reese give them a bright future, too.

I do not blame you if you didn't watch -- or even think twice (or once) -- about the Texans-Chargers Week 9 matchup. The Chargers are unwatchable, and the Texans are middling after coming into the season with Super Bowl expectations.

What you missed and may have missed for much of this season, though, is C.J. Stroud playing outstanding football. He threw five touchdown passes Sunday, and his highlights ranged from heart-warming ...

C.J. Stroud to Tank Dell for the TD 🗣️HOUvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/r0q9mBmr5d

C.J. Stroud and Kayshon Boutte with a 63-yard TD 👏HOUvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/d6CjZxnTHH

Lest you think "Oh, it's just the Chargers," they've actually been decent on defense this year. This was just Stroud putting on a clinic. It's been this way all year.

The Texans' 3-5 record is mostly due to a surprisingly up-and-down defense and major struggles on the ground. DeMeco Ryans hasn't been great situationally, either. Even if Houston doesn't make the playoffs, Stroud's play is huge for Stroud himself -- he entered the year without an extension on his rookie deal -- and for Houston, which can feel much better about handing Stroud said extension.

On a week in which Jordan Love and Joe Burrow stole the spotlight, don't forget about Stroud.

I could leave it there, but I won't. Carson Wentz isn't the answer -- clearly. Kyler Murray has never looked comfortable in this offense. Is Geno Smith the answer? A reunion with Kirk Cousins? It can't be worse than it's been, and Minnesota simply cannot waste this defense again.

Jonah Coleman recorded 17 carries for 57 yards and a touchdown and caught all four of his targets for 31 yards in the Broncos' 26-21 win over the Panthers. He played 53 of Denver's 65 snaps, second-most of any skill-position player behind Courtland Sutton. He also played nine of Denver's 10 third-down snaps.

J.K. Dobbins, on the other hand, played just nine snaps overall, and zero on third down. After some injuries earlier this year, Coleman owns this backfield -- especially until RJ Harvey returns -- and that's a good thing.

Coleman already has as many rushing touchdowns (three) as Dobbins has despite having less than half of Dobbins' carries.

Jonah Coleman gets the @Broncos back in the end zone!DENvsCAR on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/E9pCf15J6A

Let's remember that Coleman is a fourth-round rookie, too. He should continue to get better. Denver's reportedly been shopping around for running backs, but if it doesn't land one, Coleman will emerge as an early-down bell cow (with Harvey more in the mix on late downs) down the stretch.

Just, please, Sean Payton, no more pitch plays in late-game, wind-the-clock scenarios. I think Bo Nix agrees.

We highlighted Evan Williams a few weeks ago, but that was really more about Jonathan Gannon. After a game that included an incredible interception, four pressures and five tackles, Williams gets his own slot here.

The four pressures were a season high for Williams, who blitzed a season-high eight times. On one blitz, he basically shoulder-checked Rhamondre Stevenson (a good pass-blocking back) to the side and forced a throwaway. On another, he didn't get near Drake Maye but tracked back and limited Maye's scramble to 3 yards. On his final blitz of the day, he ran right by Lan Larison and nearly got a strip sack.

Williams is a combination of a high-speed train and a bumper car attacking the quarterback. If you don't try to stop him, he'll chase you down, and when you do try to stop him, he bounces off and keeps going. He now has a ridiculous 38.2% pressure rate on 34 pass-rush snaps this season.

Oh yeah, and did we mention he can do this on the back end?

EVAN WILLIAMS OH MYGBvsNE on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/0UorFkoL2o

Evan Williams, man. pic.twitter.com/HWzHimna0E

Good player. Really, really good player. All-Pro player.

It was a rough week for the NFC South. The Falcons got shellacked by the Bengals in Madrid, the Panthers lost at home to the Broncos, and the Buccaneers wasted five Bears turnovers in a loss in Chicago. The division's lone winner -- the Saints -- got an uninspiring 23-22 overtime win over Shedeur Sanders and the Browns. A failed two-point conversion is all that stood between the NFC South and an 0-4 week.

The 2026 NFC South is the only division ever with every team at least two games below .500 through Week 9. The Panthers and the Saints are 3-5, and the Buccaneers and the Falcons are 3-6. The combined 12-22 record is on pace to be the third-worst by any division since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger.

SportsLine currently does not project any NFC South team to reach eight wins. There's never been a seven-win playoff team in the 17-game era (since 2021).

But SportsLine projections also has every team reaching at least six wins, setting up for some major late-season drama. Remember last year, when the Buccaneers beat the Panthers to take the NFC South lead in Week 18, only for Carolina to win the division thanks to a tiebreaker because the Falcons beat the Saints the next day? Yeah, prepare for some weirdness.

#2592. Prisco's NFL Week 10 Power Rankings: Top 5 remains same, Bengals and Packers surging thanks to MVP candidates

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Run the ball. Run the ball. Run the ball.

That's all we ever hear about NFL offenses. If you don't run the ball, you are dead.

Let's take a look at the Cincinnati Bengals and Green Bay Packers. They don't run it well at all. Yet both enter Week 10 as legitimate Super Bowl contenders. Why? They can throw the heck out of the football.

They are the top two passing offenses in the NFL, with the Bengals averaging 285.5 yards per game and the Packers right behind at 279.7. Both have averaged over 300 the past three games.

Run games? The Bengals are 30th in rush yards per game, while the Packers are dead last. Neither is close to 100 yards per game, although their numbers are slightly up over the past three games. Neither team averages 4.0 per rush; the Packers are at 3.0, which ranks 31st in the league.

Both will have to run it better when they need to run it late in games, but, for now, having Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow and Packers quarterback Jordan Love sling it around is the way these teams need to play.

I jokingly say that neither should ever call a run play until they are leading late in games. Ok, so I'm half-joking. But you get the idea. If they keep playing with the foot on the pedal, with two big-play quarterbacks, each with a pair of down-the-field receivers, they will be tough to beat.

Both are now in my top 10 of the Power Rankings, with Green Bay moving up to No. 10 this week, with the Bengals a few spots ahead at No. 7.

Staying there for both of them will mean continuing to play the same style of football, which means not allowing the old, tired run-it folks to influence play-calling. Play to the strengths and don't get caught up in the adages about running the football.

Run the ball? Not these two. Nor should they —and both just might ride the right arms of their quarterbacks to a Super Bowl.

#2590. Bronny James faces uncertain NBA future after Lakers assign him to G League

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Lakers assigned Bronny James and rookie Cameron Carr to the G League on Thursday, the team announced. James is no stranger to the Coachella Valley Lakers, having spent time with them across his first two seasons. Still, such an early G League assignment isn't exactly an encouraging start to his third NBA campaign.

James, the 22-year-old son of LeBron James, played for the Lakers in the playoffs last season out of desperation due injuries, but when the team has been closer to full strength, he has failed to earn more than spot minutes in his first two NBA seasons. He struggled mightily in the preseason this year, as he shot just 4 of 16 from the field. And while he has always been a defense-first player, his size -- 6-foot-2 and 210 pounds -- has limited his upside on that side of the floor.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us, but I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games," Lakers coach JJ Redick said in October.

Despite those preseason struggles, James survived final cuts as the Lakers ultimately waived former No. 17 overall pick Dalton Knecht to get their roster down to 15 players. The move was relatively surprising considering their draft status. While both Knecht and James have fallen short of the team's hopes for them, Knecht was a former first-round pick who had at least held a consistent rotation role early in his rookie season. He fell off after a failed trade to the Charlotte Hornets, but teams typically like to give their own first-round picks as many opportunities as possible to succeed.

Knecht has since signed a two-way contract with the defending NBA champion New York Knicks. He appeared in his first game on Wednesday, a blowout win over the Chicago Bulls, and he notched 10 points in 16 minutes. By comparison, James has scored four points in 12 minutes spread across five appearances this season.

James was drafted in 2024 and became the first player in NBA history to share the court with his father. Now the elder James is a member of the Philadelphia 76ers, and both teams are doing well after their separation. The 76ers have the NBA's best record at 8-1, and the Lakers aren't far behind at 7-2. But with his father gone and the Lakers thriving in his absence, the younger James is in a somewhat precarious position moving forward. His name carries less weight with the organization than it once did, and a team with championship ambitions isn't going to be willing to wait on the development of a second-round pick forever.

James' contract is guaranteed through the end of this season, but not guaranteed afterward. If he doesn't show progress quickly, he could be a trade candidate at the deadline or simply not retained after the season.

#2589. NFL Week 10 picks and score predictions: Lions run over Patriots in Germany, Bengals survive

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I just got back from the NFL game in Spain, and I think I should probably start going more often, since Week 10 ended up being my best week of the year for picks.

I went 14-1 straight up, and yes, I should probably just retire at this point, but I don't want to retire while I'm on top; I want to retire when I hit rock bottom, which might actually happen this week. Speaking of rock bottom, I went to McDonald's four times while I was in Spain, and let me just say, I only went there because Madrid had the nicest McDonald's I've ever seen. I mean, just look at this place.

I'm now starting to understand why those Falcons players went to McDonald's. This is like the nicest McDonald's I've ever seen in my life. Wouldn't put it past Madrid to have a Michelin rated McDonald's #Bengals #Falcons #Spain https://t.co/w8WixT6iN2 pic.twitter.com/TMAeeXm9Fk

There were also people tailgating inside of a Taco Bell.

Taco Bell is in fact a mad house. NFL fans everywhere. Nothing like a pregame cheesy gordita crunch. #Bengals #Falcons #Spain #Madrid https://t.co/0uAafegmaM pic.twitter.com/cpjfyWy33X

If you need just one reason to ever visit Spain, tailgating at Taco Bell has to be it. Unfortunately, there's no game in Spain this week, so there will be no tailgating at Taco Bell, but there is a game in Germany, and it will be the final NFL game of this year that kicks off at 9:30 a.m. ET, which is definitely for the best, because I've reached my maximum limit for 9:30 a.m. ET games.

The Patriots and Lions will be playing in the early game on Sunday. So who's going to win? Let's get to the Week 10 picks and find out.

Alright, now let's get to the picks for real

Based on everything I've seen from the Commanders, I already know exactly how this game is going to play out: Washington is going to keep this thing close until the end only to lose (or tie) because no one in the organization has any idea what to do in any key late-game situation.

For instance, let's go back to Week 5 when the Commanders pulled off one of the all-time worst late-game gaffes in a tie with the Giants. Washington had the game won. All Jayden Daniels had to do was literally anything except what he actually did.

The Commanders can't get the play off in time and this game ends in a tie pic.twitter.com/WmPp6q5hU0

Look at the Giants players in that clip. They're celebrating. When the other team is CELEBRATING a tie, that means you lost.

Surely Daniels and the Commanders learned their lesson, right? Wrong. In their Week 9 game against the Rams, they needed a 32-yard touchdown on the final play, but instead of throwing it in the end zone, Daniels threw the ball five yards past the line of scrimmage because the Commanders apparently thought they were going to be able to lateral the ball to each other all the way into the end zone. There's a reason that never works.

With the game on the line Jayden Daniels can’t get the ball out of his hand. pic.twitter.com/2D8I1YWsiA

Now, you could blame Daniels for this stuff, but ultimately, it falls on the coaching staff. In the Rams' game, Daniels said he was just running the play that was called. In the Giants' game, someone on the coaching staff should have made it clear to everyone on the field that the clock has to come to a stop on that play, whether it's a spike or a player running out of bounds.

So what does this mean for this game? It means that the Commanders are actually playing decent football and if their coaching staff doesn't let them down, I think they have a good chance of winning. The Giants are beat up at quarterback, they're beat up at running back, and they're surviving by the skin of their teeth. Four of their five wins have come by one score. Good teams win close games -- are you taking notes, Commanders -- and I'm starting to feel like the Giants might be a sneaky good team.

To me, this is arguably the most fascinating game of Week 10. If the Commanders lose, their season is all but over, but if they win, they'll be right back in the NFC East race. I feel like this is a pick I'm going to regret as soon as I make it, but I'm taking the desperate Commanders.

With this game being played in Munich, I feel like this would be the perfect time to answer the one question that has been on all of our minds over the past few months: Who would win a beer-chugging contest between Mike Vrabel and Dan Campbell?

With these two guys heading to the beer capital of the world, there's no reason not to find out. And to be honest, based on how the Patriots have been playing recently, Vrabel could probably use a few beers right about now. I'm not in charge of scheduling events for the NFL in Germany this week, which is probably for the best, but if I were, I would rent out the Hofbrauhaus and then give both Campbell and Vrabel one full stein of beer to chug. Instead of a coin toss on Sunday, this is how we would decide who's getting the ball first.

I was at the Hofbrauhaus once and it took me an hour to finish my beer. The Germans were definitely laughing at me.

What's the record for most beers drank in one sitting here? I think I'm going to try to break it. pic.twitter.com/UQ5kOtxyPL

The Germans might be laughing at the Patriots, too, if they can't turn things around this week. Vrabel is known as one of the smartest defensive-minded coaches in the NFL, but he hasn't figured out how to stop any NFC North teams. The Patriots have faced two NFC North teams this year and not only have they gone 0-2, but they're surrendering an average of 37.5 points per game. Yikes.

The NFC North is so good that I might not pick against any of their teams for the rest of the season unless they're playing another NFC North team. If you've looked at the NFL standings at any point over the past 24 hours, you may have noticed that the NFC North is arguably the best all-around division in the NFL this year and possibly ever.

All four teams are at least three games over .500, which is the first time that's ever happened through the first nine weeks. Oh, and did I mention that the NFC North is 20-4 against all other divisions. They are destroying everyone. On the other hand, you have the Patriots, who are 3-1 against AFC East opponents, but 2-3 against everyone else. The Patriots have had one of the worst passing defenses in the NFL over the past several weeks, and now, they have to face off against a QB in Jared Goff who ranks in the top five in passing yards per game this year.

The Lions might put up 50 points. The good news for the Patriots is that even if the Lions do put up a 50-burger, New England might still keep up. Detroit has given up the MOST passing yards per game this year (260.9), so Drake Maye could certainly get some turkey carving practice for Thanksgiving here by carving up the Lions' defense. That being said, I've decided not to trust Maye against good teams.

The Patriots have faced six opponents this year with winning records, and in those games, Maye has thrown 11 interceptions to nine touchdowns. Based on how I think this game is going to go, Vrabel might need a Hofbrauhaus beer after it's over.

Deshaun Watson did not play in Week 9 for the Browns, but there's no chance he's going to miss this game. This is the ultimate revenge, though, I can't say for sure whether this is more about the Texans trying to get revenge on him or he's trying to get revenge on the Texans. Actually, now that I'm thinking about it, there might not be any revenge involved at all here.

Since trading Watson to the Browns in March 2022, the Texans have made the playoffs three times, and they've won their division twice. On the other hand, Watson has been injured for the majority of his time in Cleveland; he's won just 14 games since 2022, and the Browns have paid him roughly $14.5 million per win. If Tom Brady had earned $14.5 million per win, he would have made over $3 billion in his career. Do you know how many Hofbrauhaus beers you could buy with that money?

The worst part for the Browns is that they're still in QB purgatory, which is basically where they've been since returning to the NFL in 1999. Although Watson is playing well this year, especially late in games, I'm not sure that's a good thing. If he somehow leads Cleveland to the playoffs, the Browns might actually talk themselves into re-signing him, which doesn't seem like a great idea.

Anyway, this genuinely does feel like a game that's going to boil down to Watson vs. the Texans. Watson has been sacked more times than any other QB in the NFL this year (33), and he'll be facing a defense that leads the NFL in sacks (29). That's a recipe for disaster. There have only been three games all season where a QB has been sacked at least eight times: Two of them were Deshaun Watson (vs. Jets in Week 5 and vs. Steelers in Week 8) and the other one happened on Sunday with the Texans sacking Justin Herbert eight times.

Watson might get sacked 10 times in this game.

When I look back at the scores from Week 1, the most shocking result might have been the Vikings' 39-22 win over the Packers. One reason it was shocking is that I'm not even sure the Vikings have scored 39 points since that game. The other reason it was shocking is that the Packers became the first team in 12 years to lose by at least 17 in a game where they held a double-digit lead in the second half.

If there are two things I'm convinced about in this game, it's that the Vikings are NOT going to score 39 points (or even half that number) and the Packers are not going to blow a double-digit lead (and that's mainly because I don't think they'll have a double-digit lead).

This matchup will be giving us strength vs. strength: The Vikings have the NFL's top passing defense and they're going to have to figure out how to slow down Jordan Love, who leads the NFC in passing yards per game (290.9). Love is on quite on the hot streak right now: He's thrown for at least 270 yards in five straight games, which is something that not even Brett Favre ever accomplished. That's right, the young gunslinger is out-slinging the Ol' gunslinger.

Love has been hot because he has two receivers he completely trusts: Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. Those two BOTH went over 150 yards in Week 9 and they both had a touchdown. Do you know how many Packers' receiving duos have hit those numbers in the same game over the past 80 years? ZERO. Golden and Watson were the first ones.

One downside for the Packers in this game is that they won't have Josh Jacobs, but that might not actually be a downside, since they didn't have him in Week 1 and Love still threw for nearly 400 yards.

The Vikings started 6-0, but they're now in the reality check portion of their schedule: They're coming off back-to-back losses (Lions, Bills) and with the Packers and 49ers coming up, that losing streak could be at four in a row before Thanksgiving.

PICK: Packers 20-17 over VikingsUPDATE (Nov. 10): The Vikings just made a trade for Kirk Cousins, but that does NOT change my pick. I'm still rolling with the Packers.

After spending nearly an entire week in Spain, the Bengals are back in the United States, and this time, they have to face their toughest opponent of the year: The NFL scheduling department.

For Sunday, the NFL scheduling department has put the Bengals in a situation where no team has ever won.

The Bengals will enter Week 10 after playing in Madrid, and they face a Steelers team coming off a bye. This will mark just the sixth time in NFL history that a team coming off an international game has had to play a team coming off a bye, and uh, I have some bad news for everyone in Cincinnati: The team coming off the international game has gone 0-5 (and 0-4-1 against the spread). Also, NFL teams are a combined 13-1 coming off their bye this year.

And just when you thought it couldn't get any worse for the Bengals, I have more bad news: The team coming off the international trip has averaged just 15 points per game, and the ugly part is that they've been outscored 83-37 over the first three quarters in those five games. I feel like the Bengals should file a protest with Roger Goodell. I'm not sure that would actually do anything, but maybe it would guilt the NFL into never doing this to another team ever again. Oh wait, it's too late for that because the Lions will be in the same situation next week.

The problem with this situation is that the team returning from Europe usually needs a brief adjustment period. The jet lag after the flight back to the United States usually lasts a day or two, which means it can impact practice for your next game.

These two teams met back in Week 3 and the Steelers won because they exploited two weaknesses in the Bengals defense: Cincinnati struggles to stop the run (Jaylen Warren went off for 127 yards) and the Bengals struggle to cover tight ends (Steelers tight ends combined to make five catches for 97 yards). Overall, the Steelers offense simply played its best game of the season. They finished with 411 yards. They have not topped 365 in any other game.

I have a hard time seeing that happen again. If anyone can end this 0-5 international curse, it's Joe Burrow. He's playing quarterback at a higher level than anyone right now, and he's going to be out for revenge. Not only are the Bengals playing at home in prime time, but they're wearing their white tiger helmets, and I'm not picking against the white tiger helmets.

Chiefs 27-20 over FalconsJaguars 31-16 over TitansColts 19-16 over DolphinsPanthers 23-20 over SaintsBills 30-20 over JetsSeahawks 27-17 over RaidersRams 23-16 over Cardinals49ers 31-24 over CowboysRavens 20-16 over Chargers

Best pick: Bengals over Falcons. Last week, I predicted that the Bengals would score exactly 34 points and win the game in Spain and guess what happened? The Bengals scored exactly 34 points and won the game in Spain. When the Bengals left for Madrid last week, Joe Burrow wore a Pikachu hoodie on the flight over, and there's no way you're letting yourself be photographed in a Pikachu hoodie unless you're 100% sure that your team is going to win. As soon as I saw that photo, I was 100% sure the Bengals were going to win.

Off to Spain to catch ‘em all. pic.twitter.com/RLkWSboeRf

The twist here is that Pikachu isn't even Burrow's favorite Pokémon, and the only reason I know that is that someone actually asked him that exact question on Sunday.

Things you don't see every day: Joe Burrow got asked his favorite Pokémon in his post-game press conference. #Bengals pic.twitter.com/f1d4Y2rZGY

That's why we need more games played abroad. The international reporters aren't afraid to ask the hard-hitting questions.

Worst pick: Browns over Saints. I only missed one pick last week -- THIS ONE -- so I have to put this game here even though I don't even think it was a bad pick. There were at least five different occasions where I thought the Browns were going to win this, but this is the Browns we're talking about, so they eventually found a way to blow it. The one thing I didn't take into account is that the Browns' defense seems to be getting worse every week.

Everyone will understandably be discussing the #Browns quarterback situation today.The real concern for this season is the defense that continues to regress each week. pic.twitter.com/wTQfgdibRN

At the rate things are going, the Browns are going to give up 700 yards to the Colts in Week 17.

Finally, if you guys have ever wondered which teams I'm actually good at picking, I'm going to start sharing that information every week from now through the end of the season. Here's a quick look at my best and worst teams when it comes to picks this year.

Team: I'm 8-1 picking this year (Straight up): Patriots, Eagles, Jaguars (7-1), Dolphins (7-1), Commanders (6-1-1)My worst teams this year (Straight up): Bears (3-6), Buccaneers (3-6), Browns (3-6)

Every other team is somewhere in the middle.

You can find John Breech on Facebook, TikTok or Twitter, and if he's not doing one of those things, he's probably trying to round up some friends to see if they want to tailgate at the Taco Bell by his house this weekend.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

Barring any miraculous surprises, we're destined for a dramatic baseball offseason filled with questions about the future of the sport. It is basically a foregone conclusion that MLB will face a work stoppage at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. The lockout is coming. The real uncertainty surrounds how long it will last. That is the absolute biggest question that we hope will be answered sooner rather than later.

Collective bargaining negotiations will likely bring fundamental changes to the Major Leagues, whether it's the landmark institution of a salary cap, a shorter regular season, or numerous other proposed moves.

Surely, we will get tired of CBA talk before long. So what about the actual baseball? We have questions about free agency and the trade market, too, as Hot Stove season heats up. Our Dayn Perry explained why one of the weakest free agent classes in modern history could still go down as a groundbreaking one.

Get ready for the biggest weekend of the college football season to date. Five ranked matchups. Two top-10 showdowns. CFP implications galore. Now that the selection committee has weighed in with its first rankings of the year, we know which games it will have its eyes on the closest and how those marquee contests will reshape the resumes of the teams involved.

There is not a bigger game on the slate than No. 1 Miami at No. 11 Notre Dame. Although the Malachi Toney injury shook up the Heisman Trophy race and will undoubtedly play a role in determining whether the Hurricanes can stay unbeaten and perhaps knock the Fighting Irish out of the postseason race, Miami still has the edge at the offensive skill positions. That's why our Brandon Marcello picked the nation's top team to beat a 5.5-point spread.

Speaking of 5.5-point spreads, Tom Fornelli's Six Pack of picks includes another one with a prediction for No. 5 Alabama at No. 14 LSU.

We put No. 2 Georgia on upset alert, and the Bulldogs' trip to face No. 10 Ole Miss is among the other games we picked ahead of this colossal Saturday of football. Here are our predictions:

This week's international game is among the five biggest matchups on Sunday, mostly because it is a dangerous spot for the Bengals against a Falcons team that is similarly in the hunt for a spot in the playoffs. Cincinnati is a three-point favorite, but should it be? Joe Burrow's offense is on upset alert against a defense that gets James Pearce Jr. back from suspension this week.

Our Tyler Sullivan would not be surprised if Bijan Robinson bounces back in a big way against a Bengals unit that was just gashed on the ground by the measly Titans.

Don't let last week's scoreless effort fool you; the Falcons continue to play good offensive ball when they are not battling torrential downpours. That's why our Jordan Dajani picked the upset in Madrid.

#2585. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

#2584. NBA relegation zone predictions: Ranking the 7 worst teams in the race to avoid the bottom of the standings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When the NBA reformed the draft lottery, it did so with the hopes that all 30 teams would be somewhat competitive. But two weeks into the 2026-27 season, that isn't proving true.

Five teams have just a single win so far this season, and in many cases, those wins are only coming when they play one another. The Los Angeles Clippers have only beaten the Sacramento Kings. The Chicago Bulls have only beaten the Milwaukee Bucks. The Kings' only win came when the Dallas Mavericks rested Kyrie Irving.

No matter how the incentive structures are designed, the NBA will always have a handful of very bad teams. Some teams are poorly run. Some teams are besieged by injuries. Some teams are simply in transitional stages of their roster builds. The old NBA was designed to make bad teams good quickly. The new one is designed to make it harder for teams to bounce back from the bottom.

As part of last spring's lottery reform, the three worst teams in the league are now punished for losing. In the new 3-2-1 lottery format, the seven best teams to miss the Play-In Tournament get three lottery balls each out of the 37 available ones, while the three worst teams each get only two. In theory, that should create an all-out war to avoid the bottom three. In practice, well, we'll get into that shortly.

For now, as the bottom of the league is starting to take shape, let's take a look at our relegation zone candidates. While injuries could certainly create more of them as we go, seven teams stand out as reasonable threats for a bottom-three record so far this season. We're going to rank them from least to most likely to land in the relegation zone, with the top three teams being our official picks to take that lottery hit in May.

Remember, this is not merely a ranking of the NBA's worst teams. It's who is likeliest to land in the bottom three of the standings, a necessary distinction for reasons you're about to find out.

There isn't a more dumbfounding team to watch in the NBA right now than the Jazz. For four years, Utah was a smart, well-run team that lost because the front office did everything in its power to deprive its coach of talent. Well, coach Will Hardy is allowed to win now. It just isn't happening.

The inventive, flowing offense of years past is sputtering. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson isn't making jumpers and can't get to the rim. Players needed for size and defense -- like Josh Okogie and Jaxson Hayes -- are killing the offense. Everything is running through Keyonte George because he's the only player on the floor creating consistent advantages. He's not a true point guard, and the lack of passing on the floor right now is palpable. Their lone victory came by a single point at home against the New Orleans Pelicans. Not exactly inspiring.

Any dreams of a 50-win, top-six seed season died with the Walker Kessler trade. This team is screaming for anyone who can screen and rebound. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will help, and eventually, Jaren Jackson Jr. will take the floor again, too. You'd hope Peterson eventually figures some things out. He's a No. 2 overall pick. He's too talented to struggle this much unless the medical issues that plagued him at Kansas are persisting. There are reasons to believe this will get better. The Jazz should eventually be at least competitive.

But we're barely into November and even their more modest, post-Kessler Play-In ambitions already seem to be on life support. The Western Conference is far deeper than it looked a month ago and the Jazz are digging themselves a hole they're going to struggle to climb out of. This is a bad defensive roster even at full strength, and if the offense is this disjointed, the postseason just isn't on the table. After a four-year tank, that's a real concern in Utah. Even sniffing the relegation zone, given the time spent even getting to this point, is a borderline disaster.

The Suns come in ahead of one-win Utah -- and the two-win Orlando Magic they just beat -- because those teams have more substantial reinforcements incoming. The Suns will benefit greatly from the eventual return of Mark Williams, if only because, at this stage, Khaman Maluach just is not ready to play serious NBA minutes. But Williams isn't, say, Jaren Jackson or Paolo Banchero. Phoenix's problems are internal.

They were the first team of the season to leak displeasure to the press, with Chris Haynes reporting that the locker room is frustrated over the lack of a point guard. There's a fair bit of statistical evidence suggesting the Suns could address that problem by benching Jalen Green for Collin Gillespie. Eventually, Green's performance will force the issue. If your value is derived entirely from scoring and you're averaging 12 points on 41-22-69 shooting splits, you won't be long for anyone's starting lineup.

The bigger problem here is the loss of last year's defense-and-hustle identity. The Suns only just surrendered the NBA's 30th defensive ranking to another team on this list, and their deflections, loose ball recoveries and offensive rebounding are way down. As of this writing, they're the worst rebounding team in the NBA. Many of the players responsible for last year's identity are playing less than they did last year. Green simply isn't a defense and energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who they gave up yet another unprotected first-round pick to get.

Devin Booker is slipping. The shotmaking bar on superstar-level value for a guard who never makes plays nor gets to the rim at an elite level is almost impossibly high. He basically has to be a high-volume 3-point shooter making close to 40% of his attempts to justify his supermax deal. He hasn't come close to that in years. He doesn't quite have his old burst, either, and after the Bridges trade, the Suns are down to very few remaining draft assets with which they can improve. There's probably enough talent here that the Suns will eventually be able to eke their way to 30 or so wins, but the early returns here are pretty discouraging.

Here's where we take our first real step down in terms of roster talent. The bottom five teams are simply worse than the remaining 25. There's no All Star-level talent here, like George in Utah or Booker in Phoenix. Michael Porter Jr. made his case a year ago, but his volume is down with Julius Randle on the roster. With the Nets, Randle has been largely inefficient and is turning the ball over more than ever. Only three teams turn the ball over more frequently than they do.

They're attempting to sacrifice high opponent 3-point volume for minimizing attempts at the rim. It's working in terms of volume, but once anyone does get to the rim, they're scoring there with impunity because Brooklyn simply doesn't have a reliable, individual rim protector. They're among the most frequent fouling defenses in the NBA. Last year's No. 8 overall pick, Egor Dëmin, is already hurt and has all but abandoned shooting inside the arc. Young guards, no matter how much promise they show, are usually bad. The goal of this season is to develop several of them. Mikel Brown Jr. and the improving Nolan Traore are years away from what they'll eventually become.

Here's where we really have to start talking about incentives. Brooklyn owes its first-round pick to the Houston Rockets. Now, the Jazz and Suns owe their first-round picks out as well, but under different circumstances. The Suns won't control their own pick again until the actual sun burns out, so what happens to their picks isn't really their concern. The Jazz have picked in the top five two years in a row, so their pick, currently owed to the Memphis Grizzlies, can't land there again, and will therefore have a clean slate next year. But the Nets, who are several years away from winning meaningfully barring something unforeseen, probably want to avoid having their pick land in the top five, as teams are forbidden from ending up there three years in a row, or, in the worst-case scenario, coming in at No. 1, which would bar them from picking there in 2028.

The Nets are, in other words, incentivized to lose, which is exactly what this system was supposed to prevent. Now, they can't go about it as brazenly as tankers of the past have, as commissioner Adam Silver now has expanded powers to punish teams for tanking. But the NBA can't stop them from, say, trading useful veterans like Porter at the deadline. Brooklyn didn't do so a year ago when it should have, so this will be something to watch when February rolls around. If the Nets keep Porter, they're probably good enough to duck the relegation zone. If they move him, well, getting in there may not be the goal, but it would be a potentially helpful byproduct.

Considering the Nets traded for Randle in June, though, it seems as though Brooklyn, to the delight of Houston (which walks away with six lottery balls between Brooklyn and Phoenix in this scenario), intends to try to win. There are possible reasons for that ranging from culture-building to job security, but until the Nets show their hand, we'll leave them out of the bottom three for now.

Here's a sobering thought: of the seven teams we're covering in this space, the Kings are the only one that fits into the relegation zone system as intended. They don't owe their pick out to another team. They aren't on any consecutive high picks clock. They're just a bad team trying to rebuild organically. They want high draft picks, which means they don't want to be in the bottom three.

They might even be willing to trade a small asset to improve at the deadline for this purpose if necessary. If nothing else, they have the salary to do so. Between Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter, they have over $70 million in expiring money to dangle if doing so makes sense. Wins tend to be elusive in Sacramento, but the Kings actually want them.

They are unfortunately ill-equipped to get them. The 2026-27 Kings are quite frankly one of the strangest teams ever assembled. Former All-Star Domantas Sabonis is playing 36 minutes a game and attempting fewer shots than Precious Achiuwa. Darius Acuff Jr., meanwhile, has the second-highest usage rate any rookie has posted in NBA history, behind only Joel Embiid. He has higher usage this season than Cade Cunningham and Jalen Brunson.

The Kings aren't playing like a team whose goal is to win. They are playing like a team whose sole goal is to fast-forward through Acuff's developmental curve. That's not a crazy decision given their circumstances, but as we've addressed with Brooklyn, young guards can be productive without being especially helpful when it comes to winning. Acuff is taking shots that players like Brunson and Cunningham spend whole careers earning the right to attempt, and he is understandably far worse at actually converting them. Veteran teammates don't tend to enjoy watching rookies chuck bad shots, and without a good defender in sight, it's not as though the Kings can win on the other end of the floor. They're going to be on the bubble here. We just have three better candidates.

The ball-handling deficit here is bleak. Only the Charlotte Hornets are turning the ball over more, and nobody is even close when it comes to points allowed off turnovers. Considering Darius Garland's perpetual issues staying on the court, things are only going to get harder from here. Getting Brandon Ingram back from his partially torn Achilles will help, but he's much more of an individual shotmaker than someone who can lift an entire offense. They're struggling to generate anything near the rim as well, ranking 24th in paint points thus far. They're defending better than most of this group, a byproduct of Jeff Van Gundy's presence on their bench, but even that is at risk because of those pesky incentive structures.

The Clippers obviously owe their own first-round pick to the Oklahoma City Thunder. That isn't especially relevant, but we should note that the Clippers owe their top-three protected pick to the Philadelphia 76ers in 2029 through swap rights, and they'd probably prefer to avoid starting that top-five clock now because consecutive top-five picks would ensure they have no chance of keeping their 2029 selection.

More importantly, though, the Clippers were just stripped of five first-round picks for circumventing the salary cap. That puts them at an enormous draft capital deficit moving forward. There's no way the Clippers can recoup all of that lost value, but it makes plenty of sense for them to trade veterans for whatever value they can get in the name of setting up their future. Players like Brook Lopez, Kris Dunn, Max Strus, Derrick Jones Jr. and Rui Hachimura are all in their primes and could net positive value back in the right trades.

Since the Clippers have nothing to lose by getting relegated this year, it would likely behoove them to cash in these players for whatever value they get. If they do so, they're going to wind up in pretty rough shape down the stretch.

From a team we know circumvented the cap to a team we think very well might have. The Bucks are currently being investigated for the contract they gave Gary Trent Jr. over the summer. And the fact that he has now been DNP-CD'd in six of Milwaukee's eight games certainly doesn't help their case. If they lose picks, they're incentivized to try to make those up by trading away players they don't intend to keep long-term.

Even as it stands, the Bucks are just a bad team. They're a bottom-five offense and defense with no notable injuries. The roster mix is what you'd expect out of a team that just traded the best player in franchise history without receiving a premium asset in return: a jumbled mess. Half of the roster is comprised of shooting guards. They're thin enough at forward that they're still forced to start Kyle Kuzma, and their $108 million starting center, Myles Turner, is averaging single digits. The young players are years away. The old players are years away from the versions of themselves that warranted the minutes and money they're currently receiving.

None of this is especially surprising. It's the first year of a rebuild, and the Bucks won't control their own pick again until 2031. They're in no rush here, and the Pelicans, who control Milwaukee's pick this year, stand to lose draft value because of it.

The Bulls have been the NBA's worst team this season by a pretty comfortable margin. A brutal early schedule is somewhat to blame, of course, but they have nearly a five-point net rating gap between themselves and the No. 29-ranked Kings. They're a bottom-five defense in terms of both points in the paint allowed per game and 3-pointers made per game.

Only the Clippers give up more points off of turnovers. They rank 27th in rebounding rate. Years of steady scoring growth from Josh Giddey have seemingly been undone in two weeks. Matas Buzelis is both playing and shooting less than he did a year ago. Caleb Wilson is exploring the studio space in all of the messy ways you want a top rookie to do so. They're shooting just over 27% from 3-point range.

So the Bulls have the basketball end of the equation covered... but they also have the incentive side to consider. Remember, Wilson was the No. 4 overall pick in June. That means that another top-five pick in 2027 locks them out of the top five in 2028. The 2027 class is considered historically weak, but 2028 is expected to be stronger. Realistically, the Bulls probably don't expect to be any good next year, either. The last thing they should want is to risk getting stuck with a middling 2028 pick because they land at No. 5 in 2027.

Chicago is already terrible and has good reason to try to stay that way. Wilson has an incredibly bright future, but the present is understandably bleak.
