#2554. Vikings trade for Kirk Cousins: Minnesota turns to familiar face to salvage its season, Raiders begin new era

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Minnesota Vikings may have just solved their quarterback crisis.

Minnesota traded for veteran Kirk Cousins on Tuesday in the run-up to the NFL trade deadline, CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz reports, sending the Las Vegas Raiders their 2027 third-round NFL Draft pick in exchange. The 6-2 Vikings have lost consecutive games and are at risk of wasting an all-time defense with atrocious quarterback play, as seen Monday night when Carson Wentz went 8-for-25 with two interceptions.

The move puts Cousins back in purple -- he spent six seasons with the Vikings -- and also hands the keys to the Raiders to No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza, who has been sitting behind Cousins.

Cousins is 4-5 in his nine starts for the Las Vegas Raiders this season, completing 64.1% of his passes at an average of 7.4 yards per attempt, with 20 touchdowns against eight interceptions. He was signed to a one-year deal this past offseason to start ahead of and mentor Mendoza but with the Raiders sitting behind the eight-ball in the playoff picture and the Vikings desperate for even adequate quarterback play (the injured Kyler Murray did not light the world on fire, either) the two teams worked out a trade that makes sense for both sides.

Cousins previously spent six seasons with the Vikings. He went 50-37-1 as the starter, completing 67.9% of his passes at 7.6 yards per attempt, with 171 touchdowns and 55 interceptions. Minnesota went to the playoffs twice in those seasons, with Cousins going just 1-2 in his three postseason games.

Cousins originally signed signed a fully-guaranteed, three-year, $84 million contract with the Vikings in 2018. He signed a two-year, $66 million extension in 2020 and a one-year, $35 million extension in 2022. Minnesota allowed him to play out the final year of his contract in 2023, a season during which he tore his Achilles just prior to hitting free agency.

Rather than re-signing with Minnesota, Cousins signed a four-year, $180 million contract with the Atlanta Falcons. However, the Falcons drafted Michael Penix Jr. with the No. 8 overall pick mere months after he signed, seemingly putting an expiration date on Cousins' tenure as the starter.

He struggled during his two seasons with the Falcons, leading the NFL in interceptions during the 2024 campaign and entering 2025 as the backup behind Penix. After Penix suffered a knee injury, Cousins was named the starter for the remainder of the 2025 season and seemingly proved enough that the Raiders were willing to sign him after he was released by the Falcons.

Now, Cousins may return to Minnesota with the charge of leading the 6-2 Vikings back to the playoffs, where they'll hope to have more success than they did during his first tenure with the team.

The Vikings have started Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz under center this season and they have gotten dreadful play out of the quarterback position, with their Monday Night Football loss to the Buffalo Bills hammering home just how badly they needed to find an upgrade. Murray and Wentz (and Max Brosmer) combined to complete just 60.9% of their passes at an average of 6.4 yards per attempt, with eight touchdowns and five interceptions across eight games.

Justin Jefferson, one of the best receivers in football, can't get the ball into his hands (31 catches for 393 yards and four touchdowns on 51 targets) because the quarterbacks can't make the proper reads or throws. Jordan Addison, a quality deep threat, is being totally wasted (18 catches for 277 yards and one touchdown). And the Vikings can't run the ball because nobody respects their ability to throw it.

With Minnesota's defense looking like arguably the best in the league, the level of quarterback play the Vikings were getting was, frankly, unacceptable. You can't let a defense this good to go waste.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, Mendoza got to sit behind and learn from a veteran player to whom he has some similarities for the first half of his rookie season. Mendoza has a significantly stronger arm and is much more mobile than Cousins at this stage of his career, but they are similar in their size and stature, as well as their style of play.

Mendoza has made one appearance so far this season, completing 6 of 8 passes for 48 yards at the tail end of a blowout loss against the New England Patriots. He's got Klint Kubiak calling his plays and Brock Bowers catching his passes, but the run game he'll be married with has been extremely ineffective so far, which will put a lot of pressure on him to carry the offense the rest of the way if the Raiders cannot correct it quickly.

Mendoza will face a tough series of tests in his first few games as the starter. His first action comes against the Seattle Seahawks and the famed Dark Side defense, and he'll follow that up with a trip to Denver to take on a strong Broncos defense and then another to Cleveland to take on the Browns before the Raiders go on their bye. Post-bye week, the schedule does ease up a bit with games against the Los Angeles Chargers, Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals, but he will still face the Broncos again in Week 15, and then the Kansas City Chiefs in the regular-season finale.

#2553. Thunder trade grades: OKC swipes promising young wing Nique Clifford from the rebuilding Kings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We have our first trade of the 2026-27 NBA season, and it's a somewhat familiar one. The Oklahoma City Thunder are acquiring guard Nique Clifford from the Sacramento Kings, according to ESPN, reversing a trade that occurred during the 2025 NBA Draft. The Thunder, using a pick acquired from the Los Angeles Clippers, were on the clock at No. 24 overall, but the Kings moved into that slot to select Clifford. Now, a bit more than a year later, Clifford lands with the team whose hat he wore on draft night.

Trades this early in an NBA season are rare. Until Dec. 15, around 29% of the league is still technically untradeable because of contracts signed over the summer. However, the Oklahoma City Thunder have been ravaged by injuries so far this season. They initially planned to use their open roster spot to sign former first-round pick Ochai Agbaji, but changed course before doing so as their health issues worsened. Instead, they signed Dalen Terry to a non-guaranteed deal; they will now presumably waive him in order to take a swing on Sacramento's promising youngster. With the season's first trade done, let's grade it for both sides.

One of the advantages of working with the enormous draft surplus Oklahoma City has had since it traded Paul George to the Clippers is that it allows the Thunder to be opportunistic. Think of last February, when they stole Jared McCain from the Philadelphia 76ers for a single first-round pick. McCain was struggling through such a tough year that few teams could have afforded the risk of giving up a first-rounder for him. The Thunder obviously could, and in doing so, they got a key performer with two and a half years of cheap cost control remaining.

The thinking here is somewhat similar. The Thunder have so many second-round picks that they wouldn't miss two of them. The Kings, like the 76ers, decided they were ready to cut bait on a recent first-round pick who had shown promise far earlier than most teams would have, so the Thunder, with access to a roster spot through Terry's non-guaranteed deal and second-round picks to spare, jumped at the chance to take a swing on yet another valuable asset with several years of cost control.

Is Clifford going to be as helpful for Oklahoma City as McCain? Probably not, but there's plenty of reason to believe he can help this depleted version of the Thunder. Clifford averaged just under 13 points, five rebounds and four assists in March and April last year for a Kings team that may have been terrible, but wasn't actively trying to lose like many of its contemporaries.

His emergence as a genuine NBA Draft prospect came in his last two collegiate seasons, when he improved as a 3-point shooter playing at Colorado State. That shooting, coupled with his all-around production and bothersome 6-foot-8 wingspan as a defender, made him a promising role player prospect. Clifford does a little bit of everything. If the shots are falling, pretty much anyone could use a high-IQ, high-motor, ball-handling wing who rebounds well for his position.

This is, again, a flyer. We might find out that the Kings are giving up on him because they think he's a lemon. Think of their decision to dump Devin Carter two years after picking him in the lottery. Sometimes teams just know. Of course, the Kings are hardly the best evaluators of their own talent. See: Haliburton, Tyrese. We can't give the Thunder a straight "A" here because we've only ever seen Clifford as a productive player at the end of a single regular season for a terrible team. For all we know, the end of last season was a March mirage for Clifford. Plenty of teams fall for those.

But the cost here, for Oklahoma City's purposes, effectively amounts to loose change it found between its couch cushions. The upside is a real rotation player it can afford for several years. That's the definition of "low risk, high reward.

When the Kings drafted Clifford, he was joining a version of the team that still harbored (admittedly delusional) visions of remaining competitive. After last season, the plan changed. The Kings are moving into a rebuild now, and everything Sacramento does is geared toward the development of No. 7 overall pick Darius Acuff Jr., who currently has the second-highest rookie usage rate in NBA history. After averaging 25 minutes per game last season, Clifford has played just 50 through eight games this season. He hasn't made his shots in that small sample, which is a critical trait for anyone attempting to play off of Acuff.

Now, we're in the post-tanking NBA. In the past, we could have more fully admonished the Kings for playing veterans who won't be a part of their future, like Zach LaVine and Malik Monk, while plastering Clifford to the bench. Sacramento wants to avoid the relegation zone, so that makes a bit more sense now than it might have in the past. Couple that with the emergence of second-round pick Emanuel Sharp and former undrafted free agent Leaky Black as parts of the rotation and the impending return of Keegan Murray from a sprained ankle, and suddenly there just weren't many perimeter minutes available in Sacramento.

That all sounds fine on paper, but the NBA isn't a paper league. Players get hurt. Players get traded. Circumstances change. This was not something that needed to get settled in November of Clifford's second season. Even the Sixers waited until February to move McCain a season ago. Inevitably, there would have been more opportunities for the Kings to see what they had in Clifford as part of the Acuff-centric version of the team had they simply waited for those opportunities to arise. Sacramento simply has not earned the benefit of the doubt a team would need to justify giving up on a young player who has shown actual promise this quickly.

If this was a financially driven decision, it was still a hasty one. The Kings still had a year before they needed to make a decision on his fourth-year option. They already dropped below the luxury tax by waiving and stretching DeMar DeRozan, and there is not an immediately apparent benefit to saving another $3.3 million or so underneath it. Perhaps one will present itself later, but moving a player at this price point is typically easy enough that the Kings didn't have to rush this.

If this is a low-risk, high-reward trade for the Thunder, it's the opposite for the Kings. Best-case scenario, they're right about Clifford's value... and they get two second-round picks for someone they themselves decided was worth trading up to No. 24 to get. Not a great look for the organization. If they're wrong about Clifford and the Thunder manage to turn him into a real player as they do for almost everyone they acquire, they not only lose out on a valuable, cost-controlled asset, but become an object of ridicule for what feels like the hundredth time in the past two decades.

Last year's NBA Finals was a battle between Sacramento's former point guard (De'Aaron Fox and the San Antonio Spurs) and its former coach (Mike Brown and the New York Knicks). The 2025 Finals were nearly won by Haliburton, another former Kings point guard, and the 2023 Finals were won by Michael Malone, another former Kings coach. It's obviously unlikely that the Thunder manage to rally past all of these injuries and make it back to the Finals, and it's probably less likely that Clifford is the single reason why that would happen, but if he turns out to be a real part of a resurgent Thunder team, that will mark yet another humiliation for this Kings organization.

#2552. U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar

England wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2. After just 20 minutes, England leads 2-0. This aspect analysis focuses on the reasons behind the German attacking press’s lack of access to England’s build-up play.

The U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements. This analysis focuses on Germany’s lack of access in their attacking pressing and marking. Particularly in the first half, England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press, often gaining large amounts of space in the final third, which led to dangerous scoring opportunities.

The early deficit also contributed to Germany being unable to focus, as they usually do, on securing depth in their pressing. Instead, they were forced to put direct pressure on the ball carrier in order to force turnovers. After the equalizer to make it 2-2, Germany noticeably pressed high less frequently. Therefore, this analysis examines Germany’s pressing and marking, as well as England’s build-up play, up to the 60th minute.

One of the trends at the U21 European Championship was that many teams aimed to press the opponent’s goal kicks with a +1 player on the last line or in the space between the lines just in front of the back line. Many teams—including Germany—used man-oriented marking when closing down during goal kicks.

Since most teams build up from a 1-4-2-4 structure on goal kicks, it is equally common to press man-to-man from a 4-1-3-2 shape, with the two holding midfielders (the “sixes”) staggered vertically.

The deeper-lying holding midfielder (for Germany: Martel) acts as the +1 player, positioning himself in space based on the location of the ball. When the opponent plays through the space between the lines, he can create a numerical advantage there. In the final third, pressing is carried out against a 1-4-2 build-up using a 3-2 shape. The more advanced holding midfielder (for Germany: Reitz) typically positions himself centrally and marks the ball-near holding midfielder, while the far-side winger presses the ball-far holding midfielder.

The English side, by contrast, caused problems for the German team’s marking assignments through an asymmetrical structure. As a result, England had several options for exploiting their numerical superiority in the build-up without having to immediately play into the space between the lines.

What remained consistent was the intention to establish central possession in front of the first pressing line using different players, in order to build up play on either side. Central possession makes it more difficult for the pressing team to steer the play in a specific direction, as the passing angles from central areas are wider than those from more advanced or wider positions.

Central possession complicates the opponent’s shaping of play. Anderson’s drop frees him from Woltemade’s marking shadow and creates a numerical advantage against Nebel, who must now cover both the advanced full-back and Anderson.

The asymmetry in England’s build-up play also allowed them to repeatedly exploit their numerical superiority in specific areas tailored to Germany’s pressing structure. By stretching the positioning of their two holding midfielders (the “sixes”), Reitz was forced to cover too much ground to mark both or to shift quickly to the ball-near midfielder.

Because Germany, for the reasons mentioned above, struggled to steer the press in a specific direction, Reitz was also unable to position himself closer to the ball-near player during goal kicks. Instead, he was forced to choose which of the two midfielders to mark man-to-man.

The wide, asymmetric positioning of the holding midfielders and advanced full-backs makes both midfielders available for passes, forcing Reitz to choose whom to mark. German forwards can’t shadow the opposing midfielders, while German wingers must decide between marking the spaced-out midfielders or full-backs.

England’s positional rotations during build-up play after goal kicks were most often initiated by holding midfielder Anderson. When Germany applied pressure (as shown in the diagram above), Anderson would frequently drop into the right half-space, almost into a right-sided centre-back position, while fellow holding midfielder Scott positioned himself more centrally, and No. 10 McAtee dropped into the higher left half-space.

When Anderson instead dropped centrally in front of the goalkeeper, the right centre-back would shift wide, which in turn affected the positioning of other central players and full-backs. The specific rotations of the key players, including their reference points and triggers, are discussed in more detail in the section on England’s build-up against Germany’s high pressing.

A key aspect of England’s build-up against Germany’s pressing was their ability to evade pressure through these rotations. Since Germany used man-oriented marking, they followed the English players during these movements, which repeatedly opened up spaces that England could then exploit. For example, when McAtee dropped deep into the far-side half-space, it pulled Martel—who was defending space-oriented in the center—out of position.

The aim was to repeatedly open up central areas by drawing German players out of the middle. When the full-backs, due to the rotations, were positioned deep and wide in possession, the ball-near holding midfielder would shift outward, thereby opening the central channel. This would often be followed by an overlapping run by the full-back into the half-space, allowing him to be found deep in the center with his marker behind him and plenty of space to operate.

Luring central players out of position and opening up space through rotations is one of the core principles of England’s build-up play. It significantly disrupted Germany’s ability to gain access through their man-marking approach during pressing.

Holding midfielder Anderson’s run outward opens the center, which can then be exploited by the full-back’s typical forward run.

England also added flexibility by repeatedly using long balls from their build-up play. Especially when both the full-backs and the holding midfielders were positioned deep, they opted for long passes as soon as Germany’s wingers and central players were lured far enough out. The 2–0 goal resulted from one such long ball, which was held up by striker Stansfield and laid off to the advancing Elliott and McAtee in the half-space, who now had plenty of room to operate in the open central area.

Although these long balls weren’t always as successful as in the lead-up to the 2–0, they had the effect of preventing Germany from pressing too aggressively, as players had to remain ready to cover depth in case of another long ball. For example, Martel pushed forward only hesitantly toward the dropping No. 10 McAtee, giving him significantly more time on the ball in central areas.

Against man-oriented marking systems, it is particularly important to apply intense pressure on the ball carrier, since progression is otherwise easier than against a zonal setup.

As described, England repeatedly managed to exploit their numerical advantage in the build-up. However, Germany’s pressing approach also contributed to their lack of access. The primary aim of Germany’s pressing when closing down is less about disrupting the build-up itself, and more about winning the ball in a way that immediately creates a transition opportunity.

To do so, Germany tries to use its forwards to immediately block passing lanes to the flanks, forcing the play through the third man or central passes.

Recovering possession through intercepting a pass has the advantage over winning a tackle in that it tends to allow better control of the ball and therefore more often leads to a transition opportunity. Additionally, central ball recoveries naturally result in a shorter route to goal and, statistically, in higher-quality chances in front of goal.

However, this type of pressing also means less pressure is placed on the ball carrier, since the focus is on directing play and winning the ball after a pass. As a result, England’s ball carriers had more time to locate the free +1 player, made available through asymmetry and rotations.

In hindsight, it might have been more effective to place greater emphasis on actively disrupting the build-up itself, because England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press dangerously. At the same time, Germany had the ability to control the game through their own possession, so it wasn’t absolutely necessary to rely on winning the ball high up the pitch to create chances.

Germany’s attacking pressing operated on principles similar to those of their closing down (Zustellen). From a 4-4-2 formation with a slightly advanced Reitz on the left half-space, the forwards aimed to channel the opponent’s build-up play out wide in order to isolate the wide build-up players and engage them in man-to-man marking.

On the last defensive line, Germany aimed to maintain a +1 numerical advantage, which is why the far-side holding midfielder was usually responsible for covering depth. The German wingers were expected to track back from the full-backs to press the half-backs in the three-man defensive line that frequently formed.

Even when applying attacking pressing from open play, Germany was rarely able to gain effective access to England’s build-up. This was primarily due to England’s positional play during build-up. England’s main objective in possession is to lure opponents out of position and then exploit the spaces that open up. This goal is achieved through positional rotations that make it especially difficult for the opponent to apply effective pressure on the ball carrier during pressing. The frequency of these rotations strongly resembles the rotation-heavy positional play famously associated with Paris Saint-Germain.

The following outlines the key running paths, rotations, and reference points of the most important players.

The center-backs were rarely involved in the rotations. Only when one of the holding midfielders dropped into the build-up line did the center-backs position themselves wider. Likewise, striker Stansfield provided a fixed presence in the central deep-lying position.

Most rotations initially originated from the holding midfielders, particularly Anderson. Most frequently, he dropped into the right half-space just ahead of the center-backs. This caused the right full-back to position wider and winger Elliott to drop deeper into the half-space at the level of the last defensive line. As a result, Woltemade and Nebel had to press two players, creating a 3 vs. 2 overload.

There were also occasions when Anderson dropped into the central center-back position. Consequently, the full-backs rotated into the half-spaces, or No. 10 McAtee dropped deeper. Notably, Anderson could be found almost anywhere on the pitch. At times, he overloaded the far side, which was then followed by a role swap between him and holding midfielder Scott.

Holding midfielder Scott often positioned himself in spaces that were left vacant after a sequence of rotations. Usually, Scott remained central or rotated roles with holding midfielder Anderson. It also happened that Scott took up an open full-back position when both the winger and the full-back rotated deep.

A particularly noticeable tendency of both holding midfielders was that, when in possession, they rotated toward the flank if a wide player was positioned close to the first build-up line, making themselves available along the sideline. This had the advantage of stretching the center even further.

This was especially important because England frequently won second balls after losing possession in build-up play. In the resulting transition situation, the central area was completely free, leading to several dangerous counter-attacks through the now open middle of the pitch.

Livramento, as the right full-back, primarily oriented himself around Anderson and the right winger Elliott. In relation to Elliott, Livramento always behaved in a complementary manner: when one occupied the wide position, the other took up the half-space. It was also common for Livramento to invert and drop into the deeper half-space, with Elliott moving wider in response, and vice versa.

Anderson served as a secondary reference point. Whenever Anderson dropped back to form a wide back three, Livramento either moved inverted or stayed wide and deep. If Anderson remained central, Livramento positioned himself near the center-backs in the half-space, from where he could rotate forward into depth if the outside lane was free.

On the left side, full-back Hinshelwood and winger Hutchinson rotated according to the same principles as Livramento and Elliott. Hinshelwood also frequently inverted into the deeper half-space or moved wide and deep. Both full-backs, Livramento and Hinshelwood, often initiated rotations through their inverted runs when the ball was with the near-side build-up player.

Runs into depth, however, were usually triggered only when other players moved to offer passing options. The No. 10 McAtee also played an important role as a reference point. When McAtee (and/or Hutchinson) moved into the left half-space, Hinshelwood rotated oppositely into depth.

McAtee, as a left-sided No. 10, had a freer role. He oriented himself around the holding midfielders to occupy or overload the central area when needed. He also rotated positions with left winger Hutchinson. Often, McAtee initially moved far into the left half-space to pull defenders out of the No. 10 zone behind him and then sometimes rotated further back toward the central center-back position.

In response, either full-back Hinshelwood or holding midfielder Anderson rotated forward into depth. Alternatively, winger Hutchinson could rotate into the half-space, prompting full-back Hinshelwood to rotate wider.

The English rotations created difficult conditions for Germany’s man-oriented attacking pressing. Man-marking was repeatedly manipulated, which in turn stretched and opened up spaces. Thanks to the flexibility of long balls and superiority in second balls, England’s build-up play additionally benefited in the first half. This led to repeated situations resembling counter-attacks, as England had plenty of central space available after bypassing the press.

The early goal also forced Germany to press higher more frequently and reduced their tendency to drop deep. Germany’s pressing behavior against England’s build-up thus became one of the decisive factors influencing the course of the game in the first half.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2551. Keenan Allen trade grades: 49ers acquire WR help from Colts for Day 3 pick, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The San Francisco 49ers are adding another weapon for Brock Purdy as they gear up to race for the No. 1 seed in the NFC. At the trade deadline, the 49ers acquired veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen from the Indianapolis Colts for a sixth-round pick, per ESPN.

This is the second trade John Lynch and Colts interim general manager Ed Dodds have pulled off in the past few weeks, as the 49ers sent a fourth-round pick to Indianapolis for defensive lineman DeForest Buckner at the end of October.

Allen, who turned 34 in April, signed a one-year deal with the Colts in August and has caught 40 passes for 351 yards and one touchdown in eight games played. During Sunday's loss to the Dallas Cowboys, he caught four passes for 26 yards. Allen's 40 receptions led the Colts prior to the trade and would lead all 49ers on the season.

The 49ers were in the maket for wide receiver help, as Mike Evans (Achilles/ribs) and Deebo Samuel (hamstring) have been sidelined in recent weeks. Christian Kirk was also recently placed on injured reserve with a knee injury, where he joins fellow injured wideouts Ricky Pearsall and De'Zhaun Stribling.

Jordan Watkins, Brandin Cooks, Demarcus Robinson, KhaDarel Hodge and Jacob Cowing were Purdy's wide receivers during the 49ers' 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. Watkins led the team with 86 yards on four receptions. The injuries haven't held San Francisco's offense back yet, as through Week 9, the 49ers rank sixth in yards per game (376.8) and third in points per game (29.4). This is a well-rounded team that registered two passing touchdowns, two rushing touchdowns and a defensive touchdown on Sunday for the first time since 2022.

Allen is a six-time Pro Bowler that spent 12 of his 14 NFL seasons with the San Diego/Los Angeles Chargers, and is the franchise's second-leading receiver behind Hall of Famer Antonio Gates. He has recorded six 1,000-yard seasons and five 100-catch seasons, which is tied for third all-time.

According to the Associated Press, the 49ers have had a record seven players 30 years or older catch touchdowns this season. Only the 1998 Denver Broncos, 2007 New England Patriots and 2002 Raiders have had more total touchdowns by different players 30 or older. Imagine going back in time and telling a 49ers fan that they would have Mike Evans and Keenan Allen at wide receiver. It's true that both are older players now, but Kyle Shanahan is going to be able to get the most out of them in his system.

Allen still has some tread left on the tires, and he was the Colts' most reliable receiver despite the fact that he was not brought in to play that role. Alec Pierce has been sidelined by an ankle injury, while Josh Downs hasn't reached 25 yards receiving ever since his trade request went public. Just last year, Allen caught 81 passes for 777 yards and four touchdowns with the Chargers.

The 49ers winning this trade of course hinges on health. It remains to be seen if Evans will be able to return to 100% this season with his Achilles strain, and if Allen can remain available as well. Ultimately, the 49ers didn't have to pay a high price for a veteran pass-catcher that could upgrade the offense.

It's worth mentioning that Allen is facing a minimum three-game suspension following his OWI arrest in Indianapolis earlier this year, but we don't know when that suspension will be coming down.

The Colts are obvious sellers at the trade deadline. They are losers of five straight, fired general manager Chris Ballard last month and have already shipped off Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner and now Keenan Allen.

Allen wasn't helping the Colts win games by himself, and he was a piece Indy felt fine parting ways with prior to Tuesday's 4 p.m. deadline. The more interesting storylines to follow with the Colts come after: what will Indianapolis end up doing with star running back Jonathan Taylor and wide receiver Josh Downs?

#2550. Jayson Tatum won't give air to Jaylen Brown drama ahead of Celtics-Sixers game: 'Another game on the schedule'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- Jayson Tatum downplayed Tuesday's showdown between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which will be the first time that he and former teammate Jaylen Brown will face each other as opponents.

"It's another game on the schedule. It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one," Tatum said after putting up 21 points, four rebounds and six assists in a 117-97 win over the Milwaukee Bucks. "This one counted as one. Go get ready for Tuesday. It's a really good team, obviously. Incredible group, great coaching staff, they've been playing really well. So from that standpoint it's gonna be fun. But it's nothing more than Celtics versus Sixers."

Tatum and Brown spent nine seasons together, and led the Celtics to the 2024 championship -- the historic franchise's first since 2008 and record-setting 18th overall -- before the latter was traded to Philadelphia this summer in a blockbuster deal that brought Paul George to Boston.

Much has been made about Tatum and Brown's relationship, or lack thereof, particularly over the last few weeks.

Late last month, Tatum shared his recollection of the trade in an episode of his documentary series, "Summer of Jayson." "I was just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world," he said. In the comment section of the clip online, Brown called "cap."

Shortly after, Tatum tried to shut down any drama by pointing to all that they had accomplished together. "This ain't no f---in' Shaq and Kobe, there's no beef," Tatum said. "It's not about that. It should be more praise, and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really — that's not my thing."

Brown, on the other hand, played into the drama a few days later. "There's no beef," Brown said. "Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chop. And some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."

Now, as the first meeting between the former teammates arrives, both have tried to keep the focus on basketball.

"It's nothing to talk about. I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said after the 76ers secured a 127-121 win over the Chicago Bulls on Sunday. "Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so it's nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up. ... "We'll see how I feel when we get out there, but as of now, I got no emotion towards anything. So I'm just ready to go."

When Tatum asked if he would have a conversation with Brown on Tuesday, his response was a simple "I'm not able to tell the future," before adding that he had "no idea" if any such conversation would have to wait until after the season.

"I just know that it's the Celtics versus the Sixers. Just go out there and do my job and try to get another win," Tatum said. "Get through that, got a game on Wednesday. It's a long season. We got 72 games left. That's just the focus right now."

As for the actual basketball, both players and teams are off to terrific starts. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists on 47.7% shooting, including 39.2% from 3-point range, for the 9-2 Sixers, who sit atop the Eastern Conference. Tatum, meanwhile, is at 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists for the 8-2 Celtics, who are alone in second.

#2549. MLB rumors: Why the Dodgers could be Tarik Skubal or bust; Red Sox looking for pitching depth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.

#2548. UEFA Women's Champions League Preview: PSG Féminines vs. FC Bayern Frauen

PSG and FC Bayern will lock horns in their bid for a second UEFA Women's Champions League win of the campaign on Tuesday night. Both teams are unbeaten so far, but they have only won their matchday 2 fixtures, which left them outside automatic quarter-final spots.

Fresh from setting a new record of going 50 Frauen-Bundesliga games unbeaten, FC Bayern will look to extend their winning streak at PSG to three games. Like their last year's fixture that ended in a 3-1 win for Bayern, the game will take place at Parc des Princes.

PSG only finished with two points in the league phase last term, but they already returned home with a point from trips to Real Madrid and Manchester City this time around. And they recorded their first-ever league phase victory with a five-star performance against OH Leuven in the first day of October.

Bayern's solitary win came away from home, thanks to three late goals against Benfica in the middle of home draws with Manchester City and Real Madrid. Jose Barcala’s side squandered a two-goal lead to the WSL champions in the opening matchday, but they did the reverse against the Spanish club a fortnight ago.

While FC Bayern have won all of their first nine Frauen-Bundesliga games, PSG are already five points behind giants OL Lyonnes, who scored 48 goals in only eight Première Ligue games.

Center-back Vanessa Gilles and Kassandra Potsi didn't travel with the team after suffering injuries during FC Bayern's 3-1 win over Bremen. 19-year-old midfielder Sophie Proost is also unavailable because of illness. Regina van Eijk made her Bayern debut after Ena Mahmutovic's red card against RB Leipzig, but the number one will now regain her place for the big fixture.

As he usually does before European nights, Barcala rested key players on Saturday. Germany captain Guila Gwinn and Jovana Demnjanović are now back to full fitness, while Magdalena Eriksson, Momiko Tanikawa and Franziska Kett have all entered after the hour mark in a game the champions scored twice in the final five minutes to keep their perfect record intact.

As for the hosts, the captain Sakina Karchaoui, Anais Ebayilin and Rasheedat Ajibade are all out due to injuries.

PSG: Kiedrzynek; Isabela, Mbock ©, Samoura, Carmona; Yaya, Osteras, Echegini; Kangjinga, Feller, Elimbi

Bayern: Mahmutović; Gwinn, Eriksson ©, Ballisager, Kett; Amani, Tanikawa; Dallman, Harder, Bühl; Demnjanović

#2547. Cover 32: What every team should do at 2026 NFL trade deadline, plus game balls and gaffes from Week 9

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There was an elephant in the room during Week 9: the 2026 NFL trade deadline.

Was it just me, or did Tuesday's deadline loom over everything? With each development, it felt as if it crystallized whether or not a team should buy, sell, or hold at the deadline. Moreover, it was hard not to watch these games through the lens of which players could be dealt and playing on a new squad by this time next week. That's what makes this weekend -- the week before the trade deadline -- so fascinating.

There's an odd finality that takes over as there are no more games to further analyze a team for what they need or should sell off. Now, it's all in the hands of the front office to either improve themselves for the stretch run or potentially move an expendable piece to help themselves down the line.

As we wrap up Week 9 and barrel towards the deadline, now is as good a time as ever to give some snap impressions on every team in the NFL and how I think they should operate before 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday.

How Game Balls work: Six are awarded to standout players from the slate of teams that won their contests, and only one player on a team can get a game ball.

Chase was unstoppable in Madrid in Cincinnati's convincing 34-17 win over the Falcons. No matter what Atlanta tried to do to slow down the Bengals star receiver, they were left in the dust. This was his second straight game with at least 10 catches, 100 yards receiving, and a touchdown. That also gives him 13 such games in his career, which is the second-most in NFL history.

BURROW. JA'MARR. TOUCHDOWN. CINvsATL on NFL NetworkStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/hxTp4hwro5

Lamb had another prolific day as the Cowboys fended off the Colts in Indy. The wideout was targeted 16 times and turned that into 195 yards receiving, which is the second-most receiving yards in a game this season (most on the road). This was Lamb's fourth career game with at least 180 receiving yards, which is tied with Bob Hayes for the most in Cowboys history.

CEEDEE TD 🔥📺: #DALvsIND on FOX📲: Stream on NFL+ https://t.co/XM2vIx7C1d pic.twitter.com/QRTQGv4NZd

Welcome back, Myles Garrett! In his first game back since undergoing a procedure on his knee after the Week 1 opener, Garrett made his presence felt immediately. He took down Jayden Daniels three times in the 20-13 win, making the ninth career game he's tallied at least three sacks. Garrett also punched the ball free on one of those sacks on Daniels, which resulted in a Rams field goal drive right before halftime.

Myles Garrett strip sack!LARvsWAS on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/5RBIONmDIR

After cooling off over the past two weeks, Walker heated right back up in Kansas City's Week9 win over the Jets. The Chiefs back accounted for three total touchdowns in the win, which tied his career-high (2024 at Lions). Walker is the first player with five multi-touchdown games through eight games since Terrell Davis in 1998. Already, Walker is up to 1,044 scrimmage yards and 11 scrimmage touchdowns this season.

Mahomes to Walker again!NYJvsKC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/9NbsfKzOBB

We talked about this a few weeks ago; C.J. Stroud is balling out. The Texans quarterback has reestablished himself as a top quarterback in the NFL and just tossed five touchdowns in a blowout win over the Chargers. This was the second career game that Stroud posted at least five passing touchdowns and is just the second quarterback in franchise history to have multiple five-plus passing touchdown games.

C.J. Stroud and Kayshon Boutte with a 63-yard TD 👏HOUvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/d6CjZxnTHH

Jordan Love and the Packers steamrolled the Patriots in Foxborough, 45-27. The Green Bay QB totaled four touchdowns in the winning effort and was dialed in from the jump. His 372 passing yards were the third-most in any game of his career. He's also just the second Packers quarterback with at least 270 passing yards in five straight games, joining Aaron Rodgers (did it four times).

JORDAN LOVECHRISTIAN WATSONPACKERS ARE DOMINATINGGBvsNE on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/hxEPzs2KdC

CeeDee Lamb makes a diving catchHe doesn't get touchedGets up and picks up several yardsFumbles while getting tackledColts recover it after the play is reviewedFOOTBALLDALvsIND on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ApA5vJgMM4

One of the wildest plays of Week 9 came in the Cowboys-Colts matchup in the early seconds of the fourth quarter. Dak Prescott completed a deep ball to a sliding CeeDee Lamb, but Colts defensive back Kenneth Harris didn't touch him. Lamb realized he was untouched, got up, and ran all the way to the Indy 13-yard line. That's when Lamb fumbled, and the loose ball was recovered by the Colts.

Dan Quinn made another puzzling late-game decision. Thanks, in part, to a 42-yard catch-and-run by Stefon Diggs, the Commanders had the ball at the Rams' 31-yard line with seconds left in regulation and down by seven. One would think that Jayden Daniels would drop back and throw a prayer to the end zone in hopes of tying the game and forcing overtime, particularly as they were well within throwing range.

Instead, Daniels threw underneath for tight end Chig Okonkwo over 10 yards away from the end zone. After a lateral, the ball was fumbled and recovered by the Rams for the win.

The final play of Rams vs. Commanders featuring some laterals pic.twitter.com/9M7WYnoC2w

This is Washington simply getting too cute. At that point in the game, opt for the Hail Mary and hope for the best. Not even attempting a touchdown was ... interesting, to say the least.

Harrison Butker's struggles continued in Week 9 and included one of the major blunders of the slate. Just before halftime, the Chiefs lined up for a 56-yard field goal, but Butker's attempt was no good to the right. However, the Jets were called for an offsides penalty, which not only gave Butker another chance to put up points, but also inched him even closer for a 51-yard attempt. Despite the second attempt, he again missed wide right.

Harrison Butker misses back-to-back attempts in similar fashion following a penalty. Chiefs fans boo loudly as they head to halftime pic.twitter.com/F1BfHbIiPT

Butker has missed a total of 17 kicks since the start of last season, which is the most in the NFL over that span.

If you are a fantasy football manager that has Jonathan Taylor on your squad, you were vultured by Seth McGowan in the most peculiar way. During Indy's second possession of the day, Taylor brought the Colts to the Dallas 2-yard line after a 6-yard line. On the play, Taylor lost his shoe, which required him to go to the sideline. McGowan came in and scored on the ensuing play.

Jonathan Taylor loses a shoe, giving Seth McGowan a chance at a goal line carry which he converts into his first NFL touchdown! Awesome for him. Horrible for fantasy managers. pic.twitter.com/mil6bMm4mA

That was McGowan's first career touchdown.

The Saints first-round pick made his NFL debut on Sunday, but had a rookie blunder amid the team's overtime victory over the Browns. Tyson recorded his first career catch on a second-and-10 pass from Tyler Shough at the Cleveland 11-yard line, and it looked like he might score. As he dove towards the goal line, however, Tyson didn't protect the football well enough, and Browns linebacker Carson Schwesinger punched the ball free.

Carson Schwesinger punches the ball loose for a Browns takeaway!CLEvsNO on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/t5eYGIrmOM

Tyson finished his debut with four catches for 30 yards to go along with that fumble.

During halftime of the Broncos-Panthers matchup, Bank of America Stadium held a corgi race. However, after the festivities, one of the dogs went rogue and was running all over the field. The corgi, named Lennox, bobbed and weaved a number of would-be tacklers before ultimately being run down.

#2546. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Luka's Lakers look amazing, are Hornets regretting LaMelo trade?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

At the risk of tempting fate, we're coming off of a pretty optimistic week in the NBA. The late-October rush of season-altering injuries has seemingly slowed down. The quality of basketball has been excellent, and stars are making history. Things in the NBA are so positive right now that there are multiple, ongoing seven-game winning streaks that won't be featured in our winners of the week.

So... who beat out the trimmed-for-space Golden State Warriors and San Antonio Spurs? And who are our losers in a week full of winners? Let's dive into our rankings from the week that was.

No Jalen Williams. No Cason Wallace. No Chet Holmgren. And also, no losses. That's the week that the Thunder just had, first sweeping their season series with the Cleveland Cavaliers before blowing the doors off of the Memphis Grizzlies and Washington Wizards by 70 combined points. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander averaged just under 36 points in the 4-0 stretch, but the story here is Oklahoma City finding a new formula to compensate for all of these absences.

The Thunder built their historic defense around turnover generation, leading the NBA on that front in their 2025 championship season and finishing No. 2 a year ago. They've fallen to 21st as of Sunday, accepting that they simply cannot play as aggressively without their core defenders as they once did. Instead, they're selling out to protect the basket. They allowed the second-fewest points in the paint per game a season ago ... and have trimmed five of them off of their average this season. They've even started Isaiah Hartenstein and Aday Mara together in two of their past three games, though they've shared minimal possessions.

The defense may not be generating turnovers, but the offense isn't committing any either. Oklahoma City has taken its turnover-prevention offense to the extreme. The Thunder are averaging 231.6 passes per game, 10 fewer than any team in the tracking era. Only the Spurs and the Philadelphia 76ers, both healthy championship contenders, are turning the ball over less. This "no passes means no turnovers" offense only works if the individual creators are up to snuff. Gilgeous-Alexander obviously fits the bill, but now, so does Ajay Mitchell. The Thunder are scoring over 1.2 points per possession when Mitchell shoots out of pick-and-roll, good for the 94th percentile league-wide. He's scoring just under 25 points per 36 minutes, more than Cade Cunningham and just below Deni Avdija and Austin Reaves.

Oh yeah, and they made a trade with the Sacramento Kings. I'm comfortable calling any team lucky enough to trade with the Kings an automatic winner for that week, especially when they're acquiring a guard on a rookie contract. Do the words "Tyrese Haliburton" mean nothing to you, Sacramento? Nique Clifford certainly won't live up to that prematurely dealt King, but there's a parallel here to Davion Mitchell, another former first-round pick the Kings dealt who has since blossomed with the Miami Heat. You should trust no team's ability to evaluate players less than Sacramento's ... and no team's more than Oklahoma City's. If Sam Presti thinks Clifford can help the injury-ravaged Thunder, I'm inclined to believe that a price of two second-round picks is a bargain. All in all, it was about as perfect a week as the Thunder could have asked for.

He's averaging 40 points! This isn't a handful of games against terrible teams anymore. The Portland Trail Blazers have been great defensively against everyone except the Los Angeles Lakers because Luka has blitzed them for 94 points in two meetings. Of the 20 highest individual point totals so far this season, Dončić comes in at No. 1, No. 2, No. 5, No. 12, No. 17 and No. 18. The two biggest pillars of the MVP race are scoring and winning. Clearly, he's got the scoring down.

So far, winning hasn't been an issue either. The Lakers are 9-2, and it's almost exclusively because of the offense he runs. As of Sunday, the Lakers ranked 23rd in rebounding rate, 23rd in defense and 25th in turnover rate. It hasn't mattered because the offense is No. 1 with a bullet. The Lakers are roughly 34 points per 100 possessions better when he plays than when he sits, yet they were still able to pull off a critical road win over the Detroit Pistons on Sunday without him. The Lakers are a regular-season wins machine, and Dončić is the engineer.

It's not just the raw total, either. It's how this is all happening. Dončić currently leads the NBA in both 3-point attempts and free-throw attempts. When James Harden was doing that a decade ago, it was considered such witchcraft that defenders started standing behind him and guarding him with their hands behind their backs. I look forward to seeing what sort of nonsense teams concoct against Dončić if this continues. He's making 30-footers look like layups. He's giving Laker fans the sort of individual offense they haven't seen since Kobe Bryant's peak. Enjoy it. Stretches like this don't come around often.

The underlying message of the Ball trade was that the Charlotte Hornets did not think he could be relied upon as a franchise player. Given the questions surrounding his durability, his defense and even his maturity, it wasn't a crazy thought. The idea that he would fare better in a secondary role in Minnesota made plenty of sense. He and Anthony Edwards looked like one of the NBA's best duos in the season's opening week. Then Edwards got hurt, and Ball was suddenly back to being the centerpiece. How has he responded? Well, let's look at the team numbers since Edwards went down:

It's a tiny sample, but thus far, Ball is impacting his new Timberwolves teammates in much the same way he affected his former Hornets (don't worry, we'll get to them!). Everyone else's life gets vastly simpler on offense when they're fortunate enough to play with LaMelo Ball. Even without Edwards, he's more than kept the Timberwolves afloat. When Edwards eventually returns, this team is a genuine contender in the Western Conference.

With Ball, the Hornets had the best offense in the NBA from early December through the end of last season. Well, without him, they're last. By a mile. They're last in basically everything. No team has a lower true shooting percentage. No team turns the ball over. Ready for a jarring stat? We covered Oklahoma City's "no pass" offense earlier. Well, the Thunder are averaging more assists than the Hornets this season ... on 65 fewer passes per game.

The Hornets knew they were getting worse when they made the trade. It was a conscious choice: take a step back, take a few spins in the revamped lottery, accumulate assets that could be flipped later. The Hornets felt like they were destined to be a perpetual middle-of-the-standings team with Ball. They traded him in the hopes that getting worse now could make them championship contenders later.

Their fans probably could have lived with a small step back. What we've seen thus far has been a disaster. Not all of it is their fault. They've barely had Coby White or Kon Knueppel -- and Knueppel will be about another four weeks at least with a hamstring strain. Brandon Miller, the other cornerstone here who just signed a $209 million contract, is shooting 26% from 3 and below 36% from the floor because of how overburdened he currently is. A step back may have been the idea, but nobody thought it would be this bad, nor did many assume Ball would be this good for Minnesota. It doesn't change Charlotte's long-term outlook, but it makes the present that much more painful. All of the goodwill from last year's turnaround has seemingly evaporated.

We came into the season relatively certain about how the Western Conference was tiered. The Spurs and Thunder were at the top. The Lakers, the Wolves, the Houston Rockets and the Denver Nuggets would land between No. 3 and No. 6 in some order. After that? Well, no one gave much thought to the Play-In Tournament. The East was supposed to be the deep conference. That's an opinion we cycle through every four or five years. Every year is supposed to be the East's year, and then it isn't. When the Memphis Grizzlies and Portland Trail Blazers were lighting on the world on fire, it seemed as though the West's depth had triumphed yet again.

It still is, on balance. The Warriors and the Dallas Mavericks, for instance, are strongly exceeding expectations. But the early excitement over Memphis and Portland, at least, is starting to wane. The Grizzlies traded a six-game winning streak for a three-game losing streak. The Blazers walked into the hardest stretch of their schedule thus far, took a loss to the Lakers and then got smacked around by the Spurs. With two games against the Thunder coming, Portland is seemingly coming back down to Earth. For a moment there, the New Orleans Pelicans looked as though they were figuring some things out on a four-game winning streak, but back-to-back losses have them out of the Play-In picture, at least for now.

These teams are still better than we figured they'd be, and there's still a bit of wiggle room in the West. Denver, for instance, looks enormously vulnerable. But the Spurs have won eight in a row. The Thunder have righted the ship. The Lakers, Wolves and Rockets are all as good as we thought or better. For a moment there, it looked like we were due some surprises out West. For now, it seems as though order has mostly been restored.

It is still much, much too early to draw any meaningful conclusions about lottery reform, but an early topic thus far this season has been how bad the bottom of the league still is despite the removal of the tanking incentive. With almost three weeks in the books, there are seven teams with either one or two victories. Between those seven teams, there are only three total victories over teams above .500. The Kings beat the Mavericks ... without Kyrie Irving. The Orlando Magic beat the Toronto Raptors ... without Kawhi Leonard, and their victory over the New York Knicks at least came with Jalen Suggs in the lineup. If Suggs and Paolo Banchero were healthy, the Magic would likely not be in this class.

Essentially, when the worst teams are playing against the best ones at anything resembling full strength, they've been hopeless. Inevitably, a certain number of teams is just going to be bad whether or not they're trying to lose. In fact, given this year's specific outlook, it's not even clear how motivated any of these bottom-tier teams are to actually win. The relegation zone isn't a threat to the Milwaukee Bucks, Brooklyn Nets, Utah Jazz or Los Angeles Clippers because they don't actually control their own first-round picks. You could argue that being in the relegation zone would actually be advantageous to the Chicago Bulls in order to minimize their odds of getting a top-five pick in the bad 2027 draft, because doing so, in concert with their No. 4 pick in 2026, would lock them out of a top-five pick in the stronger 2028 class.

We might not see the sort of overt tanking we've gotten in years past, but the question here is whether or not that will actually matter. With so many of these teams having minimal incentives to win, will they still shut down key players midway through the season? Even if they don't, will attendance and television ratings be better for these teams down the stretch just because they're nominally trying? We're months away from even starting to get answers to these questions, but any notions that reform would create 30 competitive teams have been quickly dismissed. Even in October and November, some teams are already pretty tough to watch.
